Wages
WAY-jiz
noun
From the Old French wage, “pledge, pay,” the hire or recompense due to a labourer for his work.

📖 Biblical Definition

Wages are the hire and just recompense due to a labourer for his work, and Scripture guards the labourer’s right with a jealous care. The law of God forbids the master to withhold or delay them: “Thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour, neither rob him: the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning” (Lev 19:13). The Lord Jesus affirms the principle in the gospel, “for the labourer is worthy of his hire” (Luk 10:7), and James pronounces a fearful woe upon those who grind the poor: “Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth” (Jas 5:4). But Scripture also takes up the word to name the dreadful recompense of sin. As an honest day’s work earns an honest wage, so sin earns its own certain pay: “the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom 6:23). Here is the great contrast of the gospel: death is wages, earned and owed and paid in full to every sinner; but eternal life is a gift, free and undeserved, given in Christ. Wages thus stands at the heart of two truths — the justice that requires the labourer be paid, and the justice that pays the sinner the death his sin has earned, save where free grace intervenes.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The hire due to a labourer for his work; in Scripture also the certain recompense of sin, which is death.

WAGES, the hire or recompense due to a labourer for his work.

The law forbids withholding the hired man’s wages overnight (Lev 19:13).

The labourer is worthy of his hire (Luk 10:7).

The withheld hire of the reapers cries to the Lord of sabaoth (Jas 5:4).

📖 Key Scripture

Lev 19:13 — "Thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour, neither rob him: the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning."

Rom 6:23 — "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord."

Luk 10:7 — "And in the same house remain, eating and drinking such things as they give: for the labourer is worthy of his hire. Go not from house to house."

Jas 5:4 — "Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The oppression of the labourer robs the poor of his just hire; and the deceit of sin hides the deadly wage every sinner truly earns.

expand to see more

A double corruption attaches to this word, and Scripture rebukes both. The first is the oppression of the labourer — the withholding, docking, or fraudulent delay of the hire that is justly his. The law of God set its face against it: the hired man’s wages must not so much as remain overnight. James thunders that the kept-back hire of the reapers cries aloud, and that those cries have entered the ears of the Lord of sabaoth, who hears the poor and will avenge them. To defraud a workman of his pay, to enrich oneself on unpaid toil, is no small sin but a crime that calls down the judgment of heaven; the gospel that frees the soul does not loose the master’s duty to pay his servant justly.

The second corruption is subtler: the deceit by which sin hides its true wage. The world offers sin as pleasure and gain, never disclosing the recompense written into its very nature — “the wages of sin is death.” Sin is a labour that earns, exactly and inexorably, the death of body and soul; the sinner is paid in full what his sin has truly merited. The lie of the tempter, from the garden onward, is that the wage will not be paid, that “ye shall not surely die.” Against this stands the gospel’s sharp distinction: death is wages, earned and owed; but eternal life is a gift, free in Christ, who took the wage of sin upon Himself that His people might receive the unearned gift of life.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word comes from wage, a pledge or pay, naming the recompense due to a labourer for his work.

It is the hire justly due to a labourer for his work.
